title: Canonical natural right-adjoint tensor comparison with pinned projection isomorphisms
statement: Let $f:Z\to Y$ be a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] of Noetherian schemes [def-pc-scheme]. Choose the ambient and open derived categories [def-pc-derived-category], the derived pullback [def-pc-derived-pullback], direct image [def-pc-derived-direct-image], and shared derived tensor [def-pc-scheme-derived-tensor-structure], with arbitrary common localization universe. Assume direct image sends quasi-coherent objects to quasi-coherent objects (hRf), the tensor unit on Y is quasi-coherent (hO), and $Lf^*K\otimes E$ is quasi-coherent whenever K and E are. Fix a monoidal structure on Lf*, an adjunction $Lf^*\dashv Rf_*$, and an adjunction between the quasi-coherent restriction of Rf* and a right adjoint c. Let F be the actual full-subcategory lift of $K\mapsto Lf^*K\otimes c(\mathcal O_Y)$. There exists a natural transformation $\tau:F\to c$ such that for every K there exists an isomorphism $pf:Rf_*(Lf^*K\otimes c(\mathcal O_Y))\cong K\otimes Rf_*c(\mathcal O_Y)$ whose inverse is the pullback-adjunction mate of the inverse monoidal comparison followed by $Lf^*K\otimes\epsilon^a$. Its right-adjunction mate, after composition with $K\otimes\epsilon^{adj}_{\mathcal O_Y}$ and the right unitor, is exactly $\tau_K$. No invertibility of $\tau_K$ and no closure of its isomorphism locus are asserted.

proof.text: Proper implies qcqs. Apply the unbounded quasi-coherent projection formula to K and c(O_Y). The canonical projection map is the pullback-adjunction mate specified in the statement. Invert it to obtain pf; the inverse equation determines pf uniquely.

The projection map is natural in K by monoidal comparison and counit naturality. Compose its inverse with tensoring the right-adjunction counit and the right unitor. Take its right-adjunction mate. Naturality of the hom equivalence makes these components into a natural transformation from the concrete lift F to c, with the stated component equations. No choice from a mere existence theorem is used to define F.
